Co-infection constitutes a severe global syndemic affecting approximately 3.4 million people worldwide, in which each pathogen exacerbates the clinical course and morbidity of the other. Although combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication for both pathogens, it requires lifelong adherence and rarely eliminates either infection. A functional cure is defined in hepatitis B as sustained seroclearance of hepatitis B surface antigen for at least twenty-four weeks alongside undetectable viral DNA, and in HIV-1 as durable treatment-free virological control. The primary obstacle remains the persistence of cellular viral reservoirs, specifically covalently closed circular DNA for hepatitis B and integrated proviral DNA for HIV-1. The global distribution of dual infection is highly uneven, shaped by shared transmission routes including sexual contact, parenteral exposure, and perinatal transmission. At the close of 2024, approximately 40.8 million individuals were living with HIV-1 globally, among whom pooled prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen positivity was 8.4 percent, representing roughly 3.4 million coinfected individuals. Regional pooled prevalence reaches 12.4 percent in West and Central Africa and 9.8 percent across the Asia-Pacific region, compared to 5.1 percent in Latin America and 6.0 percent in Western Europe and North America. Independent cohort studies in Nigeria, Ghana, and Ethiopia documented coinfection rates between 10 and 15 percent, while China national treatment registry data identified coinfection in 8.7 percent of 33,861 patients. Key documented risk factors include male sex, detention, higher HIV load, lower CD4 cell counts, and lack of hepatitis B vaccination. The biological interaction between the two viruses is bidirectional and deleterious rather than a simple co-occurrence. HIV-1 infection causes severe CD4 T-cell depletion and chronic immune activation, upregulating programmed death-1 and programmed death ligand-1 pathways that induce profound T-cell exhaustion. This immunosuppressive environment impairs essential hepatitis B immune clearance mechanisms normally mediated by cytotoxic CD8 T cells, natural killer cells, neutralizing antibodies, and interferon signaling pathways. Conversely, hepatitis B infection alters the clinical trajectory of HIV-1. Coinfected patients present with lower baseline CD4 counts and elevated transaminases upon starting antiretroviral therapy, and experience slower early CD4 recovery over the initial four years. Furthermore, molecular studies demonstrate that the hepatitis B virus X protein directly enhances HIV-1 long terminal repeat transcription by interacting with host CCAAT/enhancer binding proteins and regulatory elements, confirming that hepatitis B actively modulates HIV-1 persistence. Anatomically, the human liver serves as a shared sanctuary harboring viral reservoirs for both pathogens. Hepatitis B virus establishes stable intranuclear covalently closed circular DNA within hepatocytes, while HIV-1 infects hepatocytes, resident Kupffer cells, and liver-infiltrating CD4 T cells, persisting even throughout suppressive antiretroviral therapy. Microbial translocation across compromised intestinal mucosa releases lipopolysaccharide and soluble CD14 into circulation, driving intrahepatic expression of inflammatory chemokines like CXCL10 and CCL2. Elevated intrahepatic CXCL10 strongly correlates with accelerated liver fibrosis in coinfected cohorts. Concurrently, HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp120 binds chemokine receptor CCR5 on hepatic stellate cells to promote profibrogenic signaling, while enhanced hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha and transforming growth factor-beta-1 activity exacerbates collagen accumulation. Because hepatic HIV persistence maintains localized immune activation, curative regimens must target both viral reservoirs within hepatic tissue rather than focusing exclusively on peripheral blood compartments. This severe pathogenic interplay translates into accelerated liver disease progression and heightened oncological vulnerability. Clinical data from a Spanish cohort showed that 20 to 25 percent of men living with HIV-1 developed chronic hepatitis B following acute infection, compared to only 5 percent among immunocompetent adults. Hepatocellular carcinoma incidence reaches 1.8 cases per 1,000 person-years in North American coinfection cohorts and 1.7 cases in Swiss studies. Major independent risk factors for liver cancer include age over forty years, hepatitis C coinfection, alcohol use, HIV viremia exceeding 500 copies per milliliter, hepatitis B viral loads above 200 international units per milliliter, low CD4 counts, and pre-existing cirrhosis. Although tenofovir-containing regimens significantly reduce hepatocellular carcinoma incidence, increasing patient longevity elevates the lifetime risk of cirrhosis. Furthermore, a meta-analysis encompassing 12,382 participants revealed that hepatitis B coinfection significantly increases overall all-cause mortality among individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy. In chronic hepatitis B monoinfection, curative benchmarks highlight the contrast between suppressive nucleoside analogs and immunomodulatory interventions. Approved oral agents like entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and tenofovir alafenamide clear circulating viral DNA in over 90 percent of patients within one year, yet achieve surface antigen seroclearance in only about 1 percent. By comparison, pegylated interferon-alpha strategies achieve surface antigen loss rates ranging from 3 to 65 percent depending on baseline criteria. In the OSST trial, switching from entecavir to pegylated interferon-alpha yielded 8.5 percent overall antigen seroclearance, rising to 22.2 percent in patients with antigen levels below 1,500 international units per milliliter and 77.8 percent below 200 international units. The NEW SWITCH trial recorded 14.4 percent and 20.7 percent seroclearance at 48 and 96 weeks, while the Everest study involving 15,896 patients achieved 26.4 percent loss. Novel agents such as bepirovirsen have also demonstrated meaningful functional cure outcomes. In HIV-1 research, curative strategies distinguish complete sterilizing cure from functional remission maintaining viremia below 50 copies per milliliter without antiretroviral therapy. Spontaneous control occurs in fewer than 1 percent of infected individuals, recognized as elite controllers who possess protective HLA class I alleles and effective immune responses. However, long-term remission in the Geneva patient transplanted with wild-type CCR5 cells and the second Berlin patient receiving heterozygous donor cells indicates that complete coreceptor absence is not strictly mandatory. Given the extreme risks of transplantation, scalable approaches focus on CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to disrupt CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors, successfully conferring cellular resistance against viral entry in preclinical evaluations. Alternative functional cure pathways for HIV-1 involve latency-targeting interventions, broadly neutralizing antibodies, and immunomodulatory agents. Under the shock-and-kill strategy, latency-reversing agents including histone deacetylase inhibitors like vorinostat, romidepsin, and panobinostat are deployed to reactivate latent proviruses for immune clearance, while block-and-lock approaches utilize Tat inhibitors to silence transcription permanently. Concurrently, infusions of broadly neutralizing antibodies have demonstrated clinical efficacy; the TITAN trial established that 36 percent of participants sustained viral suppression beyond 25 weeks, while triple antibody combinations achieved control in 83 percent for at least 28 weeks. Pegylated interferon-alpha also possesses dual immunomodulatory potential, producing a median viral decline of 0.61 log10 copies per milliliter in HIV monoinfection and reducing CD4-associated viral reservoirs in coinfected patients with hepatitis C. Despite these individual advancements, their efficacy and translational feasibility in simultaneous hepatitis B and HIV coinfection remain essentially untested. Translating single-infection cure models into coinfection encounters both distinct immunological opportunities and severe clinical hazards. Coinfected individuals receiving long-term suppressive tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy paradoxically achieve surface antigen clearance rates between 7 and 11 percent, exceeding 10 percent in select cohorts, well above the 1 percent annual rate seen in hepatitis B monoinfection. This phenomenon reflects immune reconstitution, where restoring CD4 counts disrupts pre-existing hepatitis B immune tolerance and provokes hepatic flares that frequently precede antigen loss. However, these hepatic flares pose severe risks of acute decompensation and fatal liver injury. Furthermore, end point assessment introduces a major ethical barrier: while hepatitis B functional cure can be confirmed on active therapy, establishing an HIV functional cure requires an analytical treatment interruption. In coinfected patients, interrupting antiretroviral therapy risks aggressive hepatitis B viral rebound, catastrophic hepatitis flares, and liver failure, and no established protocol currently exists for safe interruption. To navigate these challenges, the authors proposed a four-phase sequential framework as a hypothesis-generating model. Phase one establishes deep dual suppression through at least four to five years of continuous tenofovir-based therapy, which lowers hepatic inflammation, prevents fibrosis progression, and provides an immunological baseline without treatment interruption. Phase two applies retrospective criteria to select optimal candidates, prioritizing patients with surface antigen levels below 1,500 international units per milliliter, favorable genotypes like genotype B, CD4 counts above 350 cells per cubic millimeter, and previous immune flares. Phase three investigates combination immunotherapy by adding pegylated interferon-alpha for 24 to 48 weeks, potentially alongside checkpoint inhibitors, Toll-like receptor 8 agonists, or latency-reversing agents under strict safety monitoring. Phase four involves consolidation, flare monitoring, and hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, restricting analytical treatment interruption exclusively to clinical trials with rigorous rescue protocols. Advancing this conceptual framework requires dedicated clinical trials and validated biomarkers specifically evaluated in coinfected populations. Early-phase trial designs such as AIDS Clinical Trials Group A5394 illustrate the meticulous safety protocols and biomarker-driven endpoints required for evaluating combination immunotherapies. In accordance with 2025 European Association for the Study of the Liver guidance, clinical studies must evaluate emerging hepatitis B biomarkers, including quantitative surface antigen, hepatitis B core-related antigen, and circulating viral RNA, in parallel with assays quantifying intact HIV reservoirs. Furthermore, single-cell multiomics technologies are needed to simultaneously track virus-specific T-cell responses within the same coinfected individuals, while genotype-guided strategies must address differences across viral lineages. Because historical clinical trials routinely excluded coinfected individuals due to toxicity concerns, the authors conclude that close collaboration between hepatology and HIV research communities is essential to replace theoretical extrapolations with robust clinical evidence. records.content: LOADING ERROR LOADING Vaccination rates in children and babies are dropping across the United States. This is made clear by current measles outbreaks in states such as Pennsylvania, New York, Wisconsin and more. Now new research , published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, shows that parents are not only opting their babies out of the measles vaccine, but also the hepatitis B vaccine. The study was conducted by researchers from Callen-Lorde Community Health Center in New York and Truveta, a healthcare data company. Researchers analyzed the medical records of more than 1.3 million babies and found that as of June 2026, 65.6% of newborn babies were vaccinated against hepatitis B in their first 24 hours of life, down from 80% in 2022. While the drop in hepatitis B vaccination rates started in 2023, the continuing decline comes at a time when Trump-era federal vaccine advisers voted to remove the hepatitis B vaccine from the childhood vaccine schedule. (The move is currently blocked by an American Academy of Pediatrics lawsuit , so the hepatitis B shot still remains part of the schedule.) “I find it unfortunate that vaccination rates are declining, because this inevitably means that rates of hepatitis B infection will ultimately rise, and lives will be permanently affected,” said Dr. Leslie Treece , a pediatrician in Tennessee. Treece is not involved with this study. “Prior to 1991, we used to recommend vaccination only to ‘high risk’ groups. In spite of this, there were still about 24,000 cases per year of hepatitis B infection in infants [in the U.S.],” Treece said. “After adopting universal newborn vaccination, the case number dropped dramatically to a few hundred or less cases in the US per year.” Hepatitis B can be lifelong and chronic, and can lead to liver cancer and liver failure. “With hepatitis B, this is especially worrisome because it is a lifelong, chronic disease with no cure, leading to liver failure and liver cancer later in life,” said Dr. Zhen Chan , a pediatrician at Zarminali Pediatrics in Washington, D.C. Chan was not involved with this study. “Both of these diseases can lead to early death,” Chan added. Hepatitis B is not always lifelong and chronic, but it is more likely to be the earlier someone is infected. This vaccine is given to newborns because transmission during birth ― or within the first 24 hours of life from an infected mother ― carries the highest risk of chronic hepatitis B infection and later risk of cancer and liver disease, explained Dr. Alexandra Yonts , a pediatric infectious diseases specialist at Children’s National in Washington, D.C. Yonts is not involved with this study. “About 1 in 4 children with lifelong infection eventually die of cirrhosis or liver cancer if untreated. The longer a baby is left unvaccinated, the higher the chance of getting infected,” Chan said. Sollina Images via Getty Images Hepatitis B vaccination rates are declining in newborns in the United States. Hepatitis B is rare; it’s estimated that 640,000 adults have chronic hepatitis B, but that further points to the power of vaccination. “Many families will question how their baby would even get hepatitis B when the rates are so low. I usually explain that rates are low because of the vaccine itself, and the lower the vaccination rates in the community, the greater the risk of getting the disease,” Chan said. “The safety data supports giving the hepatitis B vaccine at such an early age. Completing the full series gives a baby about a 98% level protection against the disease,” Chan added. Not only does the vaccine prevent babies from infection when they’re young, but it goes on protect against hepatitis B infection when they reach adulthood, said Dr. Rick Malley , a senior physician in pediatrics, division of infectious diseases at Boston Children’s Hospital. Malley is not involved with this study. “The idea of preventive vaccination for diseases that the individual might really only encounter much later in life is one of the great successes of hepatitis B vaccination,” Malley said. “By immunizing children early, we were really preventing ... transmission perinatally, and also providing protection later in life.” The consequences of a decline in hepatitis B vaccination won’t be seen for some time. “There are all these understandable instances of confusion that people might have when they hear their healthcare provider tell them one thing, and then they go on the internet, or they get exposed to some video that tells them exactly the opposite,” said Malley. It’s not surprising that people pause the recommended vaccine schedule when they see conflicting messaging online, he noted. “Unfortunately, we know that when that happens, the likelihood that an individual will get a vaccine-preventable disease increases significantly,” Malley said. The current measles outbreaks throughout the U.S. are just one example of this, and the now decline in hepatitis B vaccination is another, he added. “I think now with hepatitis B, the consequences of of these drops in vaccinations ... may not be observed quite as quickly as we, unfortunately, are seeing with the measles outbreaks,” Malley said. “So, that is also confusing in a way because the consequences of this may not be seen for a while.” “And I think, broadly, it also points to another bit of a problem in the field of vaccines, which is that ... vaccines are really victims of their own success,” he said. Most people don’t know someone who had polio. Most people had not heard about measles until the current outbreak in the U.S. “Trying to convince the public that the reason they don’t know about these terrifying diseases is precisely because of vaccination is a bit of a hurdle,” he said. In the end, “the benefits of preventing chronic Hep B infection and complications of liver disease and liver cancer far outweigh any minor risks ... of vaccination,” Yonts said, adding that there are no major adverse effects or side effects of the vaccine. “Giving this vaccine to every baby ... is the most equitable and responsible thing we can do for our population,” Yonts added. “We shouldn’t make babies (and the future of our country) pay the price of failings of our healthcare for pregnant women.” | Submit a tip

The molecular approach seamlessly combines reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification with Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated identification inside a custom-engineered sealed tube. Hepatitis B virus infection remains a pressing global health concern requiring reliable diagnostic strategies. Circulating hepatitis B virus RNA has been proposed as a valuable surrogate biomarker that directly reflects the transcriptional activity of covalently closed circular DNA within virus-infected hepatocytes. By mirroring intrahepatic covalently closed circular DNA activity, measuring circulating viral RNA aids clinicians in assessing therapeutic efficacy and evaluating antiviral treatment response in infected individuals. To establish the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA detection system, the investigators designed specific loop-mediated isothermal amplification primers and 5′-phosphorylated guide DNAs targeting hepatitis B virus RNA. The research team systematically evaluated and optimized critical diagnostic parameters governing the performance of the molecular assay. These optimization procedures established the precise reaction temperature required for reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification. Additionally, the investigators systematically calibrated the reaction duration necessary for Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated cleavage to ensure reliable target recognition and enzymatic activity. Analytical validation demonstrated that the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA assay achieved an ultrasensitive limit of detection of five copies per reaction. Furthermore, analytical specificity testing showed that the platform displayed no cross-reactivity against other microbial species, confirming that the designed primers and guide DNAs selectively identify hepatitis B virus RNA without generating false-positive background results. The entire diagnostic workflow was successfully completed within ninety minutes from initial processing to visual result interpretation. This timeline comprises approximately forty-five minutes for hepatitis B virus RNA preparation, thirty minutes of reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification, ten minutes for Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated cleavage, and less than two minutes for visual readout on the gold nanoparticle-based lateral flow biosensor. The clinical feasibility of the diagnostic platform was assessed through serum specimens obtained from chronic hepatitis B patients. When tested on these clinical serum samples, the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA assay demonstrated one hundred percent concordance with the standard reference method, quantitative real-time PCR for hepatitis B virus RNA, confirming its clinical diagnostic reliability. The authors concluded that these preliminary results demonstrate considerable promise for the accurate and convenient monitoring of chronic hepatitis B infections. Furthermore, the novel closed-tube platform establishes an important technical foundation for developing point-of-care molecular diagnostics targeting other infectious diseases, particularly for healthcare settings in resource-limited regions. Here are five stocks we like better. Precision BioSciences plans to advance PBGENE-HBV into Phase II to test whether it can eliminate enough hepatitis B cccDNA for a viral cure. The study will evaluate the treatment alone and followed by bepirovirsen, with initial Phase II data expected in the second half of 2027. Duchenne muscular dystrophy data are expected in 2027: three-month biopsy results from roughly the first three patients could arrive around the second quarter, with the first patient's 12-month biopsy data expected in the fall. The first patient had no serious adverse events reported, and the safety board supported continued dosing. After a recent $125 million raise, the company reported cash of more than $200 million and said its runway extends into the fourth quarter of 2029. Precision BioSciences (NASDAQ:DTIL) plans to advance its hepatitis B gene-editing treatment into a Phase II study and expects initial biopsy results from its Duchenne muscular dystrophy program in 2027, executives said at a Jefferies conference. Chief Scientific Officer Cassie Gorsuch said the hepatitis B study will test whether the company's treatment, PBGENE-HBV, can reduce enough of the viral material known as cccDNA to achieve a viral cure. Chief Operating Officer Alex Kelly said the company expects to begin seeing Phase II data in the second half of 2027. → Gold Is Down 35%—Is the Bull Case Broken or Just Bruised? Kelly also said Precision had $108 million in cash as of Sept. 30 and recently raised $125 million, taking its cash balance above $200 million. He said the company's cash runway extends into the fourth quarter of 2029. Hepatitis B program moves toward Phase II Gorsuch said 25 patients had received PBGENE-HBV in the repeat-dose Phase I study, with 59 administrations across the group. At a recent liver meeting, the company reported that six patients with at least six months of follow-up after their pregenomic RNA, or pgRNA, became undetectable continued to have undetectable levels. → Plug Power Near $1: A Hydrogen Turnaround or Another False Start? The company views pgRNA as a primary biomarker for the treatment's effect on cccDNA, the hepatitis B viral material it is designed to eliminate. Gorsuch also said the first e-antigen-positive patient treated in the study had a 3.7-log reduction in pgRNA to undetectable levels at the 0.4 mg/kg dose selected for the next phase. Despite the encouraging biomarker results, Gorsuch said the remaining question is whether the treatment has eliminated enough cccDNA to produce a viral cure. The Phase II study is intended to answer that question. Story Continues → Alphabet's Most Tempting Valuation Signal May Be Its Most Misleading The study will assess PBGENE-HBV alone and followed by the antisense treatment bepirovirsen. The monotherapy arm will test for viral cure, defined in the discussion as undetectable HBV DNA after treatment is stopped; the combination arm will assess functional cure. Gorsuch said the company sees a potential benefit from reducing viral burden before administering bepirovirsen. Patients in the combination arm will need to meet bepirovirsen eligibility criteria, Gorsuch said. Kelly said Precision had not yet discussed a partnership with GSK but was prepared to purchase bepirovirsen for the study. For patients stopping nucleoside therapy, Gorsuch said normal liver enzymes and fully suppressed HBV DNA are baseline safety considerations. She said regulatory guidance calls for six months off nucleoside treatment to demonstrate an approvable endpoint. Kelly said any withdrawal of therapy in Phase I would be handled case by case, with the larger Phase II study expected to provide more consistent data. Duchenne study awaits biopsy results Precision's Duchenne muscular dystrophy program uses its ARCUS gene-editing technology to remove a region of the dystrophin gene and aims to restore a near full-length dystrophin protein. Gorsuch said the targeted region is mutated in up to 60% of children with the disease. The first patient in the Phase I/II FUNCTION-DMD study had no serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest, Gorsuch said. An independent data safety monitoring board reviewed results through eight weeks after treatment, saw no concerning safety signals and endorsed completing dosing of the first part of the study, she said. Kelly said three-month biopsy data for approximately the first three patients could be available around the second quarter of 2027. The second patient had been enrolled and the third was being screened, he said. Gorsuch said the company believes dystrophin expression above 5% could be therapeutically meaningful, but emphasized that any protein increase must ultimately be linked to functional benefit. Kelly said the first patient's 12-month biopsy data could arrive in the fall of 2027. Gorsuch said the 12-month point would also be more appropriate than three months for beginning to assess functional improvements. About Precision BioSciences (NASDAQ:DTIL) Precision BioSciences is a biotechnology company developing gene-editing therapies using its proprietary ARCUS platform. The platform is designed to make targeted changes to DNA and is being applied to investigational treatments for genetic and infectious diseases. The company's programs include PBGENE-HBV, an investigational therapy designed to target hepatitis B virus DNA, and PBGENE-DMD, a gene-editing program for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These candidates remain in development and are not approved treatments. The investigation combined an umbrella review of existing systematic reviews with a de novo meta-analysis of duplicate-free primary studies to clarify reactivation risks that clinicians encounter during immunosuppressive therapy. Hepatitis B virus reactivation represents a preventable yet inconsistently managed complication for individuals undergoing immunosuppressive regimens. While routine antiviral prophylaxis is widely recommended for surface-antigen-positive patients, clinical uncertainty and questions regarding real-world applicability have persisted for patients with resolved infection, those receiving emerging immunotherapies or biologics, solid organ or stem cell transplant recipients, and diverse regional patient populations. To evaluate the existing body of evidence, the research team deployed a structured two-level analytical framework. The first level conducted a review-level synthesis, systematically searching six comprehensive research databases for systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between January 2014 and March 2025. Investigators formally appraised the methodological quality of the retrieved reviews using the AMSTAR-2 tool and calculated the degree of overlap among reviews using the Corrected Covered Area metric. The second level of the framework consisted of a de novo meta-analysis directly aggregating data from primary clinical studies identified across the search results. After removing duplicate entries across overlapping reviews, investigators extracted data from 275 primary studies and applied a random-effects model to compute pooled incidence estimates. Findings across both tiers were subsequently assembled into structured evidence maps categorized by serological markers and specific drug exposures. Across the ten included systematic reviews and meta-analyses, the authors identified critical methodological limitations, noting that the overall methodological quality of the review-level evidence was low or very low. A qualitative narrative synthesis of this literature demonstrated that the observed risk of viral reactivation was highest among individuals positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, followed by individuals displaying a surface-antigen-negative and core-antibody-positive serological profile. The subsequent de novo meta-analysis of the 275 original primary studies provided specific pooled quantitative risk estimates across these distinct serological groups. Among individuals who were surface-antigen positive, the pooled incidence of hepatitis B reactivation was 11.44 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 9.17 percent to 13.86 percent. In contrast, patients with resolved infection defined by negative surface antigen and positive core antibody status demonstrated a pooled reactivation incidence of 0.99 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.41 percent to 1.74 percent. Additional subgroup evaluations within the resolved hepatitis B cohort indicated that patients lacking surface antibodies experienced higher reactivation estimates than those with detectable surface antibodies. The data also confirmed that prophylactic antiviral therapy was associated with a lower incidence of viral reactivation among surface-antigen-positive patients undergoing immunosuppressive treatment. The investigators emphasized significant statistical heterogeneity across all conducted subgroup analyses, cautioning that these summary figures reflect an inherently diverse evidence base rather than exact incidence rates directly generalizable to every bedside setting. Furthermore, direct comparative evidence comparing different antiviral agents remains insufficient, as does conclusive evidence demonstrating prophylactic benefit in patients with resolved infection, highlighting the ongoing need for targeted research. Why some parents aren't giving their children the Hep B vaccine WCVB US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:27 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 7:08 PM EST Nov 25, 2026 Editorial Standards i Livia Daggett Digital Curator Less than two-thirds of newborns got hepatitis B shots in first half of 2026 Updated: 7:08 PM EST Nov 25, 2026 Editorial Standards i Livia Daggett Digital Curator Less than two-thirds of newborn babies in the U.S. were vaccinated against hepatitis B this year, a drop of nearly 15% from 2020, according to a new study. In a report published this week in the journal NEJM Evidence, researchers found that after reaching an average of 80% from 2020 to 2022, rates of vaccination against hepatitis B for newborns began to decline in 2023, falling to 65.6% in 2026. Advertisement Past video coverage of related study on drop in vaccination rates above. This is the first look at hepatitis B birth vaccination rates after the Centers for Disease Control in December 2025 ended its longstanding recommendation that all babies get the vaccine at birth. Hepatitis B is a virus that can damage the liver and lead to lifelong health problems. The vaccine against it protects against short-term illness and a life-threatening infection called chronic hepatitis B, which is the most common form among newborns. Babies can be exposed to hepatitis B from their mothers, during labor or in the early days of their lives. People often don’t know they are infected with the virus, making it more difficult to prevent transmission. In December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, a committee within the CDC that earlier that year had its members replaced with new ones, stopped recommending HBV vaccination for all newborns. It instead recommended parents of babies whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B make a decision with their healthcare providers. The vaccines were still recommended for babies whose mothers tested positive or had an unknown status. CDC panel rolls back hepatitis B vaccine recommendation for newborns “The bottom line is confusion creates inaction among parents,” Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, an author of the study and a former leader at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Wall Street Journal . “It’s as clear as mud what to do because you have public messaging that sheds doubt on the effectiveness of the hepatitis B vaccine.” The change in guidance for hepatitis B vaccination came amid sweeping changes to childhood vaccination recommendations pursued by the Trump administration. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has a history of sowing doubt about vaccines, and after taking office, he dismissed the members of the CDC’s vaccine policy committee and appointed new ones. And in January 2026, the CDC cut its list of vaccines recommended for every child from 17 to 11, one of the biggest changes to childhood disease prevention in decades. However, this study found that hepatitis B vaccination rates for newborns started to drop in 2023, before the CDC’s change, though the decrease continued afterward. The authors said the continuing drop likely reflects “continuing vaccine hesitancy and confusion among parents” after the changes to newborn hepatitis B vaccine recommendations. A separate study on newborn hepatitis B vaccinations from earlier this year pointed to the decline coinciding with a “period of heightened public discourse in the US regarding childhood vaccination following the COVID-19 pandemic.” The American Academy of Pediatrics, the largest professional association of pediatricians in the U.S., continues to recommend that babies receive the shot at birth. American Academy of Pediatrics releases updated children's vaccination recommendations According to a 2024 CDC report , among children born in the U.S. from 1994 to 2023, routine childhood vaccinations will have prevented approximately 508 million lifetime cases of illness, 32 million hospitalizations and 1,129,000 deaths, as well as resulting in direct savings of $540 billion and societal savings of $2.7 trillion. During that same time period, the hepatitis B vaccine that the CDC no longer recommends for all children prevented 6 million cases of hepatitis B and 940,000 hospitalizations, the CDC report said. The report found that hepatitis B birth vaccine doses fell even among babies born to mothers who did test positive for hepatitis B, dropping from an average of around 97% to 98% in 2018-2025 to 93.9% during the first half of 2026. The authors said that drop could “potentially indicate distrust of medical interventions even beyond recommendations.” Get the Facts: The US overhauled its childhood vaccination schedule. HepB-vaccination_NEJM-Evidence_graph-A A new Truveta led study published NEJM Evidence on Nov. 24, 2026, analyzed de-identified electronic health records from more than 1.3 million infants, found that hepatitis B vaccination received within one day of birth declined from approximately 80% in 2022 to 65.6% by June 2026. The decline began in 2023, nearly three years before federal vaccine advisers changed the longstanding recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth. Bellevue, Wash., Nov. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Hepatitis B vaccination among US newborns has fallen sharply in recent years, including among infants born to mothers with hepatitis B infection, according to new Truveta research published in NEJM Evidence. The study, which analyzed de-identified electronic health records from more than 1.3 million infants, found that hepatitis B vaccination received within one day of birth declined from approximately 80% in 2022 to 65.6% by June 2026. The decline began in 2023, nearly three years before federal vaccine advisers changed the longstanding recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth. Researchers also identified a troubling decline among newborns at greatest risk of infection. From 2020 through 2025, between 97-98% of infants born to mothers who tested positive for hepatitis B received the vaccine at birth. During the first six months of 2026, that rate fell to 93.9%. "The hepatitis B birth dose was designed to protect every newborn, including those whose mothers may not know they're infected," said Nina Masters, PhD, MPH, Principal Research Scientist at Truveta and the paper's lead author. "No screening system is perfect. That's why it's so concerning to see vaccination declining across the board, even among babies whose mothers have tested positive for hepatitis B." Hepatitis B can be transmitted from mother to child during birth, making timely vaccination especially important. Yet despite widespread prenatal screening, researchers found that approximately one in 10 pregnancies had no recorded hepatitis B test. Applied to roughly 3.6 million births in the US each year, that screening gap could affect an estimated 360,000 newborns annually. Based on the infection rate observed in the study, researchers estimate that more than 640 infants each year could be born to mothers whose hepatitis B infection went undetected during pregnancy. Masters added that these findings underscore the importance of the hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination as a safeguard against infections that might otherwise be missed. The study lands amid significant changes to US vaccine policy. In December 2025, federal vaccine advisers voted to end the longstanding recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth, followed by broader changes to the childhood immunization schedule in January. A federal judge temporarily blocked those decisions in March 2026, restoring the previous recommendations while litigation continued. Story Continues While the decline in birth-dose vaccination began well before these policy decisions, the findings raise new concerns about gaps in protection that were already emerging. "We're talking about a vaccine that has protected generations of children from a potentially devastating infection. And now we're seeing fewer newborns receive it—even those we know are at greatest risk," said Demetre C. Daskalakis, MD, MPH, a study co-author and the former director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. "These numbers aren't just a trend line. Each data point represents a real child who may be left vulnerable to a preventable disease. At a time when vaccine policy is changing, we need more evidence guiding our decisions, not less." The study, "Hepatitis B Birth Dose Vaccination in the United States: January 2018 – June 2026," analyzed de-identified electronic health records from 1,338,961 infants born to more than one million mothers. Researchers used linked maternal and infant records to examine prenatal hepatitis B screening and vaccination following birth. The study was authored by Nina B. Masters, PhD, MPH; Brianna M. G. Researchers Deyou Tang, Wensheng Yang, and Juan Fu conducted a large-scale computational evaluation of 29,153 distinct Hepatitis B virus integration sites to resolve long-standing discrepancies regarding where viral DNA inserts and how these insertions relate to the development of hepatocellular carcinoma. By establishing a normalized analytical framework, the authors identified distinct genomic preferences that separate viral insertion events occurring in liver tumor tissues from those found in non-tumor counterparts, clarifying structural and functional mechanisms underlying viral hepatocarcinogenesis. Hepatocellular carcinoma represents a primary liver malignancy with Hepatitis B virus infection serving as a predominant pathogenic driver worldwide. Chronic infection permits viral DNA to integrate directly into the host hepatocyte genome, an event recognized to promote oncogenic transformation through multiple cellular disruptions including chromosomal instability, insertional mutagenesis in key cancer genes, and cis-activation of neighboring transcripts. Despite decades of study, earlier characterizations of recurrent integration hotspots showed persistent inconsistencies beyond a few recognized genes such as telomerase reverse transcriptase and Cyclin E1. Previous investigations had also diverged regarding whether insertions favored specific functional chromatin regions or fragile sites, variations largely attributable to limited cohort sizes, tumor heterogeneity, different viral sub-genotypes, and diverse detection methodologies across independent laboratories. Discover more Cancer Order DNA Kits Find Study Aids To overcome these methodological variations and sample-size limitations, the researchers constructed a curated reference resource by assembling 36,009 raw viral integration sites from 21 published articles and the Viral Integration Sites Database. The team applied rigorous curation criteria, discarding records lacking chromosomal coordinates or valid chromosome numbers, eliminating unlocalized scaffolds and mitochondrial hits, and restricting candidate assemblies to GRCh37 and GRCh38 before systematically converting all valid loci to reference genome GRCh38.p14 via the NCBI Genome Remapping Service. Integrations located within twelve nucleotides of each other were merged into unified central coordinates, and duplicated entries from overlapping reports were eliminated. The final curated catalog comprised 29,153 unique viral integration sites, containing 12,759 sites identified in liver tumor tissues, 15,834 in adjacent non-tumor tissues, 1,151 in cell-free circulating DNA, and 290 in cell line models. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology cancer Find Cancer Care Assessing insertion density across varying chromosomal lengths required a standardized comparative metric capable of controlling for cohort-level and regional variability. The investigators developed an analytical measurement defined as the number of Hepatitis B virus integration sites per million nucleotides, abbreviated as VPM. This formula factored the site count in a given target region, the base-pair length of that region, the total integration tally across the dataset, and the specific integration tally within the corresponding tissue class. Furthermore, the baseline expected density over autosomes and sex chromosomes was adjusted by incorporating the demographic sex ratio derived from the clinical records, resulting in an expected baseline of 9.74 integrations per million nucleotides for autosomes, 5.89 for chromosome X, and 3.85 for chromosome Y. Hypothesized integration frequencies were modeled through binomial distributions and evaluated against expected distributions via Z-tests and chi-square tests. At the gross chromosomal level, viral insertion events were identified spanning nearly the entire human genome, targeting 831 of the 862 cytobands recognized in standard genomic annotations, equivalent to 96.4 percent of all cytobands. However, statistically significant insertion densities clustered in specific structural zones, with tumors exhibiting significantly elevated insertion rates compared to non-tumor tissues on chromosomes 5, 8, 17, 19, and Y. Notably, chromosome Y demonstrated an integration density in tumor specimens that was twice as high as that observed in non-tumor tissues, an observation that aligns with the established clinical epidemiological disparity showing higher hepatocellular carcinoma incidence in males than females. While centromeric regions showed an absence of viral enrichment, terminal chromosomal zones displayed strong insertional biases, with the average density in cytobands nearest to telomeres reaching roughly double the genome-wide expectation. Discover more Genomic genomics genomic Fine-scale mapping of chromosomal extremities revealed that peak viral insertion density did not reside directly at the physical telomeric ends, but concentrated preferentially within a window 100 kilobase pairs from the chromosome extremities, where tumor tissues overwhelmed non-tumor tissue rates. Within this terminal 100-kilobase-pair perimeter, integration sites exhibited asymmetric preferences, clustering unevenly toward either the short p-arm or long q-arm of individual chromosomes. The authors noted that recurring integration in telomeric vicinities involves microhomology-mediated repair processes with guanine-rich repetitive telomeric sequences, a phenomenon known to induce complex structural rearrangements, telomerase binding irregularities, extensive DNA amplification, and terminal deletions during early hepatocarcinogenesis. When examining functional genomic architecture, the team determined that Hepatitis B virus insertions were significantly enriched within CpG islands, proximal promoter regions located within one kilobase pair of transcription start sites, and 3-prime untranslated regions. Conversely, integration occurred without significant preference in chromosomal fragile regions or open chromatin regions relative to baseline statistical expectations. Proximity evaluations around CpG islands demonstrated that integration frequency was highest directly within the islands and steadily declined as distance increased outward through two and ten kilobase pairs. Tumor tissues exhibited significantly elevated insertion density in CpG islands relative to non-tumor tissues, as well as in the CpG island shores of chromosomes 4, 5, 17, 18, 19, and 21. Because CpG islands and promoters frequently harbor GC-rich short direct repeats that align with viral DNA ends during host repair, structural integration can disrupt methylation dynamics and perturb normal transcriptional control. Analysis of gene structural domains revealed that 17.96 percent of all integrations mapped to promoters, 33 percent fell within introns, and 45.91 percent localized to distal intergenic regions. In tumor tissues, proximal promoter insertions within one kilobase pair were significantly elevated compared to non-tumor counterparts. Furthermore, viral insertions concentrated disproportionately in cancer-associated genes, particularly oncogenes over tumor suppressor genes. Cancer genes accounted for 15.1 percent of integration sites restricted to tumor samples compared to only 4.6 percent of sites found exclusively in non-tumor tissues, while genes demonstrating integration across both tissue types showed an 18.6 percent cancer-association rate. Highly recurrent insertion targets included recognized drivers such as telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), lysine methyltransferase 2B (KMT2B), Cyclin E1 (CCNE1), Cyclin A2 (CCNA2), and Albumin (ALB), with insertions frequently occupying the promoter domains of TERT, CCNA2, and CCNE1 and the 3-prime untranslated region of KMT2B. To connect physical integration hotspots with transcriptional consequences, the researchers evaluated gene expression data from 371 hepatocellular carcinoma samples in The Cancer Genome Atlas, stratified into four distinct cohorts: HBV-infected tumors, HBV-uninfected tumors, HBV-infected non-tumor tissues, and HBV-uninfected non-tumor tissues. Pairwise differential expression analysis demonstrated substantial transcriptional remodeling in tumor tissues compared to rare expression changes in non-tumor cohorts. Candidate integration genes and their immediate upstream and downstream flanking genes exhibited pronounced transcriptional divergence. Specifically, the expression changes for TERT, CCNE1, and Alpha fetoprotein (AFP) were markedly amplified in HBV-infected comparisons relative to uninfected groups. Elevated AFP transcription in infected tumors was highlighted as an external regulatory effect linked to adjacent viral insertions within the neighboring Albumin locus, illustrating insertional cis-effects on neighboring gene expression. Pathway enrichment of differentially expressed genes with multiple integration events revealed pronounced alterations in critical cellular processes, including transmembrane transport, cAMP signaling, calcium signaling, and the cytochrome P450 pathway. The investigators observed significant differences in monocarboxylic acid metabolic processes and oxoacid metabolism specifically within HBV-infected comparative groups that were absent in uninfected comparisons. Functional interactions between dysregulated genes highlight converging mechanisms of hepatocarcinogenesis, wherein TERT-mediated telomere lengthening and CCNE1-driven G1/S transition promote uncontrolled cell cycle progression, while KMT2B modifications alter histone methylation and DNA repair checkpoints. Metabolic adjustments facilitated by AFP and carbamoyl-phosphate synthase 1 (CPS1) further sustain proliferative demands, establishing a multifaceted oncogenic network. The authors underscored several study limitations inherent to their data integration strategy. Because the curated dataset aggregated genomic coordinates from published literature and databases without uniform access to raw sequence reads, breakpoint-level motif signatures and microhomology sequences could not be independently reconstructed. Furthermore, technical variations across diverse sequencing platforms, library depths, patient age distributions, tumor stages, and viral subtypes could introduce detection biases. The authors also emphasized that because the Cancer Genome Atlas lacks concurrent viral integration sequencing for the same specimens, direct causal connections between specific insertional breakpoints and individual transcriptomic alterations remain preliminary, requiring targeted experimental and multi-center validation in prospective clinical cohorts. MMP9 expression distinguished all five occult hepatitis B samples from five healthy controls. Findings supported further investigation of MMP9 for early liver injury risk assessment. OCCULT hepatitis B virus infection may be associated with a distinctive blood gene expression signature, with MMP9 emerging as a potential biomarker for identifying patients at risk of liver injury, according to an exploratory transcriptomic analysis. The findings followed a clinical case involving rapid progression from genotype C occult hepatitis B infection to advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification. Occult Hepatitis B Presents Diagnostic Challenges Occult hepatitis B virus infection is characterised by undetectable hepatitis B surface antigen despite detectable viral DNA, creating challenges for identifying and monitoring affected patients. Currently, validated biomarkers for predicting liver injury or disease progression in this population remain unavailable. Researchers reported a patient with genotype C occult hepatitis B infection who rapidly developed advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. This case prompted an exploratory investigation into potential molecular markers associated with occult infection. The researchers reanalysed a publicly available transcriptomic dataset containing peripheral blood mononuclear cell samples from individuals with occult hepatitis B and healthy controls. Differential gene expression analysis was performed to identify candidate biomarkers, followed by sensitivity testing to assess the consistency of the findings. MMP9 Expression Distinguishes Occult Hepatitis B Samples The analysis identified 1,930 differentially expressed genes between the occult hepatitis B and control groups. Among these, MMP9, which encodes matrix metalloproteinase 9, demonstrated one of the strongest transcriptional signals (log2 fold change: 10.69; adjusted p=6.13×10−36). All five occult hepatitis B samples expressed MMP9 at substantially higher levels than the five healthy controls. Raw expression counts ranged from 547–25,598 in the infection group, compared with 2–8 among controls, with no overlap between groups. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated complete separation (area under the curve: 1.000), with sensitivity and specificity both reaching 100% (95% CI: 56–100% for each). However, these estimates were derived from only 10 samples and require cautious interpretation. Biomarker Findings Require Prospective Validation Sensitivity analyses further supported the consistency of the MMP9 transcriptional signal. Across 10 leave-one-out iterations, MMP9 remained among the highest-ranked genes, with consistently increased expression (log2 fold change: 10.52–10.81). The mean number of differentially expressed genes across these analyses was 1,901, with a coefficient of variation of 5%. Researchers suggested that MMP9 could represent an early-warning candidate biomarker for occult hepatitis B-related liver injury. Nevertheless, the study did not establish that MMP9 predicts future hepatocellular carcinoma, and the small discovery cohort limits generalisability. The findings also require validation in independent populations before clinical risk assessment applications can be considered. Overall, the analysis identified a promising molecular signal that warrants prospective investigation to determine its relationship with liver injury and disease progression in occult hepatitis B infection. Reference Liu X et al. records.content: The number of babies getting vaccinated for hepatitis B at birth is dropping precipitously Hepatitis B, which can be passed from mother to baby, is a liver disease that can be fatal if left untreated Join Our Community of Science Lovers! The number of babies born in U.S. who received a vaccine for hepatitis B within a day of birth has dropped sharply, according to a new study. Researchers at the health data firm Truveta and Callen-Lorde Community Health Center in New York City examined anonymized electronic health records from more than 1.3 million infants and found the percentage who received the shot within 24 hours of being born had fallen from 80 percent in 2022 to just 65.6 percent in 2026. The decline extended to babies who were most at risk: up to 98 percent of mothers who tested positive for hepatitis B got their babies vaccinated in 2022, but that had fallen to just under 94 percent in 2026, the study found. The findings were published in the journal NEJM Evidence on Tuesday. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. “The hepatitis B birth dose was designed to protect every newborn, including those whose mothers may not know they’re infected,” said Nina Masters, principal research scientist at Truveta and the study’s lead author, in a statement. “No screening system is perfect. That’s why it’s so concerning to see vaccination declining across the board, even among babies whose mothers have tested positive for hepatitis B.” Hepatitis B is a liver disease that can, if left untreated, lead to liver cancer or even death. The disease is transmissible through body fluids and can be passed from mother to baby in the womb. By extrapolating their data to the 3.6 million births that occur in the U.S. each year, the researchers concluded that as many as 360,000 infants are likely going without the shot. While prenatal screening is widely available, they also estimated that roughly 640 unvaccinated babies may be born to mothers who have been infected with hepatitis B but have not been screened. The number of unvaccinated infants is “alarming,” says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “They represent children who will develop chronic hepatitis B infections, cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancer,” he says. “They also send a clear signal to federal health leaders that they need a plan to address increasing rates of vaccine hesitancy other than misleadingly blaming it on the pandemic.” In December 2025 the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel eliminated a decades-old recommendation that the hepatitis B vaccine be given universally at birth. Instead the panel recommended parents consult with a health care provider about when to give their baby the child’s first dose of the vaccine as long as the mother has tested negative for the disease. The change quickly drew fire from public health experts, who said the decision ran contrary to the evidence and would increase infants’ vulnerability to infection. records.content: Precision BioSciences Targets Hepatitis B Cure in Phase II, Eyes Duchenne Data in 2027 3 min read DTIL −0.49% Precision BioSciences DTIL plans to advance its hepatitis B gene-editing treatment into a Phase II study and expects initial biopsy results from its Duchenne muscular dystrophy program in 2027, executives said at a Jefferies conference. Chief Scientific Officer Cassie Gorsuch said the hepatitis B study will test whether the company’s treatment, PBGENE-HBV, can reduce enough of the viral material known as cccDNA to achieve a viral cure. Chief Operating Officer Alex Kelly said the company expects to begin seeing Phase II data in the second half of 2027. Kelly also said Precision had $108 million in cash as of Sept. 30 and recently raised $125 million, taking its cash balance above $200 million. He said the company’s cash runway extends into the fourth quarter of 2029. Hepatitis B program moves toward Phase II Gorsuch said 25 patients had received PBGENE-HBV in the repeat-dose Phase I study, with 59 administrations across the group. At a recent liver meeting, the company reported that six patients with at least six months of follow-up after their pregenomic RNA, or pgRNA, became undetectable continued to have undetectable levels. The company views pgRNA as a primary biomarker for the treatment’s effect on cccDNA, the hepatitis B viral material it is designed to eliminate. Gorsuch also said the first e-antigen-positive patient treated in the study had a 3.7-log reduction in pgRNA to undetectable levels at the 0.4 mg/kg dose selected for the next phase. Despite the encouraging biomarker results, Gorsuch said the remaining question is whether the treatment has eliminated enough cccDNA to produce a viral cure. The Phase II study is intended to answer that question. The study will assess PBGENE-HBV alone and followed by the antisense treatment bepirovirsen. The monotherapy arm will test for viral cure, defined in the discussion as undetectable HBV DNA after treatment is stopped; the combination arm will assess functional cure. Gorsuch said the company sees a potential benefit from reducing viral burden before administering bepirovirsen. Patients in the combination arm will need to meet bepirovirsen eligibility criteria, Gorsuch said. Kelly said Precision had not yet discussed a partnership with GSK but was prepared to purchase bepirovirsen for the study. For patients stopping nucleoside therapy, Gorsuch said normal liver enzymes and fully suppressed HBV DNA are baseline safety considerations. She said regulatory guidance calls for six months off nucleoside treatment to demonstrate an approvable endpoint. Kelly said any withdrawal of therapy in Phase I would be handled case by case, with the larger Phase II study expected to provide more consistent data. Duchenne study awaits biopsy results Precision’s Duchenne muscular dystrophy program uses its ARCUS gene-editing technology to remove a region of the dystrophin gene and aims to restore a near full-length dystrophin protein. Gorsuch said the targeted region is mutated in up to 60% of children with the disease. The first patient in the Phase I/II FUNCTION-DMD study had no serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest, Gorsuch said. An independent data safety monitoring board reviewed results through eight weeks after treatment, saw no concerning safety signals and endorsed completing dosing of the first part of the study, she said. Kelly said three-month biopsy data for approximately the first three patients could be available around the second quarter of 2027. The second patient had been enrolled and the third was being screened, he said. Gorsuch said the company believes dystrophin expression above 5% could be therapeutically meaningful, but emphasized that any protein increase must ultimately be linked to functional benefit. Kelly said the first patient’s 12-month biopsy data could arrive in the fall of 2027. Gorsuch said the 12-month point would also be more appropriate than three months for beginning to assess functional improvements. About Precision BioSciences DTIL Precision BioSciences is a biotechnology company developing gene-editing therapies using its proprietary ARCUS platform. The platform is designed to make targeted changes to DNA and is being applied to investigational treatments for genetic and infectious diseases. The company's programs include PBGENE-HBV, an investigational therapy designed to target hepatitis B virus DNA, and PBGENE-DMD, a gene-editing program for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These candidates remain in development and are not approved treatments. The study demonstrated that CD4+ T cells from patients with chronic hepatitis B displayed elevated levels of KLRG1, accompanied by increased genomic DNA damage and telomere shortening. Alongside these cellular alterations, investigators identified prominent activation of the MRE11/RAD50/NBS1-ataxia telangiectasia mutated (MRN-ATM) pathway in CD4+ T cells from individuals with chronic hepatitis B virus infection. In persistent viral infections, T-cell senescence represents a hallmark of immune dysfunction characterized by the accumulation of DNA damage and telomere attrition, though the precise role of the DNA damage response pathway in CD4+ T cells during chronic infection has remained poorly defined. Targeted experimental interventions demonstrated that suppressing MRN attenuated ATM phosphorylation and its downstream signaling molecules. Furthermore, inhibition of ATM reduced the production of interferon-gamma and interleukin-2 in CD4+ T lymphocytes isolated from both individuals with chronic hepatitis B and healthy subjects. Discover more Find Senior Care Study Biology Check Symptoms Study Anatomy Get Tested The findings indicate that concurrent activation of the MRN-ATM pathway during chronic hepatitis B virus infection may represent a mechanism that repairs genomic DNA damage and associates with CD4+ T-cell cytokine production, although it does not fully prevent senescence. The authors noted that elucidating the relationship between this senescence-associated phenotype and the MRN-ATM pathway provides insight into the mechanisms underlying viral persistence and may inform future therapeutic strategies. In persistent viral infections, T-cell senescence represents a hallmark of immune dysfunction characterized by the accumulation of DNA damage and telomere attrition, though the precise role of the DNA damage response pathway in CD4+ T cells during chronic infection has remained poorly defined. Targeted experimental interventions demonstrated that suppressing MRN attenuated ATM phosphorylation and its downstream signaling molecules. Furthermore, inhibition of ATM reduced the production of interferon-gamma and interleukin-2 in CD4+ T lymphocytes isolated from both individuals with chronic hepatitis B and healthy subjects. The findings indicate that concurrent activation of the MRN-ATM pathway during chronic hepatitis B virus infection may represent a mechanism that repairs genomic DNA damage and associates with CD4+ T-cell cytokine production, although it does not fully prevent senescence. The authors noted that elucidating the relationship between this senescence-associated phenotype and the MRN-ATM pathway provides insight into the mechanisms underlying viral persistence and may inform future therapeutic strategies. “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Open access 慢性乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)感染仍是重大全球健康负担。核苷(酸)类似物(NAs)可抑制病毒复制并降低疾病进展,但乙肝表面抗原(HBsAg)清除仍较少见。因此,治疗目标日益聚焦于功能治愈,而持续性HBsAg清除是其核心终点。聚乙二醇干扰素α(PEG-IFNα)为有限疗程治疗方案,可在特定患者中诱导HBsAg清除。定量HBsAg是研究最为充分的治疗中标志物,第12周和第24周检测可为反应指导治疗提供依据;其他病毒标志物如HBV RNA和乙型肝炎核心相关抗原(HBcrAg)亦受关注,但其相关性随乙型肝炎e抗原(HBeAg)状态、治疗策略和人群而异。常规血液学和肝脏生化指标的连续监测证据仍较有限,且既往研究中生物标志物评估与结局判定时窗高度重叠,限制了时间先后顺序的判断。因此,早期实验室变化是否先于后续HBsAg清除,以及哪一时间区间最具信息价值,仍不明确。 研究人员在一项接受聚乙二醇干扰素α-2b(PEG-IFNα-2b)治疗的回顾性双中心队列中解决了这一问题,采用第24周里程碑设计,将早期血液学和肝脏生化变化与后续HBsAg清除相分离。 主要发现包括:第12至24周期间淋巴细胞恢复幅度更大,与后续HBsAg清除相关;该关联在校正治疗中HBsAg动力学后依然存在;纳入淋巴细胞变化后, optimism校正后的曲线下面积(AUC)由0.757升至0.805;潜在轨迹类别与HBsAg清除无显著关联。 慢性乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)感染仍是全球重大疾病负担,现有核苷(酸)类似物(NAs)虽能有效抑制病毒复制,却极少实现乙肝表面抗原(HBsAg)清除。随着治疗目标向功能治愈转变,持续性HBsAg清除已成为核心终点。聚乙二醇干扰素α(PEG-IFNα)作为有限疗程方案,可在部分患者中诱导HBsAg清除,但疗效存在显著个体差异。目前,定量HBsAg的第12周和第24周动力学是主流的反应指导标志物,HBV RNA与乙型肝炎核心相关抗原(HBcrAg)等新型标志物亦受关注。然而,关于常规血液学与肝脏生化指标动态变化的研究证据有限,且既往分析中标志物测量与结局判定在时间上高度重叠,难以确立早期实验室变化与后续HBsAg清除的先后关系。基于此,研究人员利用第24周里程碑设计,在双中心队列中系统评估了早期常规实验室指标动态对后续HBsAg清除的预测价值。 欢迎索取义翘神州凋亡检测试剂盒最新资料领 取 本研究为回顾性双中心里程碑队列研究,队列来源于天津市第一中心医院(2023—2026年)与天津市第三中心医院(2019—2026年)接受PEG-IFNα-2b治疗的成人慢性HBV感染者,共纳入269例符合里程碑条件的患者。主要技术方法包括:第24周里程碑设计与离散时间生存分析(complementary log-log模型)以分离暴露窗口与结局窗口;线性混合效应模型刻画8项常规指标(白细胞、中性粒细胞、淋巴细胞、单核细胞、血小板、丙氨酸转氨酶(ALT)、天冬氨酸转氨酶(AST)、直接胆红素(DBIL))的早期轨迹;潜在类别混合模型(latent class mixed model)识别轨迹亚型;并通过Bootstrap内部验证、校正多重比较及增量预测指标(AUC、C-index、Brier评分、连续净重分类改善(NRI)、综合判别改善(IDI))评估模型性能。 研究得出的核心结论是:第12至24周期间淋巴细胞计数的回升幅度,是后续第24至72周内HBsAg清除的独立正相关因素;该关联在校正年龄、性别、第24周log?? HBsAg及第12周淋巴细胞计数后依然稳健,且不受基线HBsAg水平、年龄、性别、HBeAg状态及治疗方案影响。将这一动态指标加入临床模型后, optimism校正的72周AUC由0.757提升至0.805,提示其具备增量预测价值。 关键技术方法概括(不超过250字):研究基于天津两家三级医院2019—2026年真实世界队列,采用第24周里程碑框架切分暴露与结局;以线性混合效应模型比较清除组与非清除组在基线、第12周、第24周的8项常规指标轨迹差异;用离散时间互补log-log生存模型评估各时间窗变化量(每1个标准差)与后续清除的风险比(HR);辅以潜在类别混合模型提炼轨迹亚型,并以1000次Bootstrap做 optimism校正,计算AUC、C-index、Brier评分、NRI与IDI完成增量预测验证;多重比较采用Benjamini–Hochberg与Holm校正。 3.1 患者特征 里程碑队列共269例,47例(17.5%)在第24周后至第72周内实现HBsAg清除。清除组更年轻(P<0.001)、体质指数(BMI)更低(P=0.001)、基线HBsAg更低(P<0.001)、γ-谷氨酰转移酶(GGT)更低(P=0.008);初始方案中富马酸丙酚替诺福韦(TAF)联合PEG-IFNα-2b占比更高(P=0.030)。其余血液学与生化基线指标组间无显著差异。 3.2 早期血液学与生化指标的纵向变化 线性混合模型显示,两组淋巴细胞均在第0至12周下降,随后第12至24周清除组回升、非清除组维持低位;组间变化差为0.325×10?/L(95% CI 0.141–0.509,Holm校正P=0.002),整体交互P=0.002(FDR校正P=0.019)。单核细胞第12至24周变化呈名义差异(Holm P=0.016),ALT交互P=0.035,但经FDR校正后均不再显著;白细胞、血小板、中性粒细胞、AST、DBIL无显著轨迹差异。 3.3 早期实验室变化与后续HBsAg清除的关联 离散时间生存模型(模型C,校正第12周起始值、年龄、性别、第24周log?? HBsAg)显示:基线至第12周无任何指标经FDR校正后显著;基线至第24周淋巴细胞变化HR=1.83(95% CI 1.19–2.83,P=0.006)但FDR P=0.074未达显著;第12至24周淋巴细胞每升高1个标准差,清除风险HR=1.93(95% CI 1.43–2.62,P<0.001,FDR P<0.001),为唯一显著项。时间异质性检验无显著差异(P=0.504)。 3.4 增量预测价值与内部验证 在267例完整数据中,加入第12至24周淋巴细胞变化后:相比仅含第24周HBsAg模型,optimism校正ΔAUC=0.060;相比临床模型(年龄、性别、第12周淋巴细胞、第24周HBsAg),AUC由0.757升至0.805(ΔAUC=0.048),C-index由0.802升至0.829,Brier由0.170降至0.159,连续NRI=0.497,IDI=0.046;校准斜率约0.54,提示预测风险偏极端。 3.5 潜在轨迹模式 潜在类别混合模型仅中性粒细胞与AST保留两类别解;白细胞、淋巴细胞、单核细胞、ALT、DBIL因类别比例<10%或分类质量不足归为单类。中性粒细胞两型均为先降后部分回升(低水平型n=238,高水平型n=31);AST两型分别为一过性升高后下降(n=241)与持续明显升高(n=28)。 3.6 轨迹类别与后续清除 校正后高水平中性粒细胞型vs低水平型HR=0.89(95% CI 0.38–2.09,P=0.781);持续AST升高型vs一过性型HR=2.01(95% CI 0.81–4.95,P=0.130)。两者均无统计学显著关联。 3.7 亚组分析 第12至24周淋巴细胞回升的HR在各亚组点估计均>1:基线HBsAg≤1500 IU/mL者HR=1.98(P<0.001),女性HR=2.18(P=0.006),HBeAg阴性HR=1.92(P<0.001),TAF+IFN组HR=3.72(P<0.001),TDF+IFN组HR=2.11(P<0.001);交互检验均不显著(P>0.05),HBeAg阳性仅1例事件无法估计。 3.8 敏感性分析 排除第24周前已清除者后中性粒细胞轨迹结论不变;岭回归校正HBsAg第12至24周降幅、HBeAg、方案后HR=1.60(95% CI 1.15–2.03);限制HBV DNA低于检测下限者HR=1.90(P<0.001);Benjamini–Yekutieli校正后P=0.002仍显著。 讨论部分总结:该双中心里程碑队列将常规实验室窗口与结局窗口在时间上分离,证实“第12至24周淋巴细胞回升”而非“基线到第12周下降”才是与后续HBsAg清除相关的信号,且在校正治疗中HBsAg后仍独立存在。总淋巴细胞计数无法区分效应/调节亚群、细胞再分布或功能活化,既往单细胞研究提示初始/记忆T细胞比例与CD8? records.title: 中国生物制药:首个慢性乙型肝炎功能性治愈疗法贝普若韦生钠注射液在中国获批上市
records.excerpt: 人民财讯11月27日电,中国生物制药在港交所公告,慢性乙型肝炎(CHB)同类首创功能性治愈疗法贝普若韦生钠注射液(商品名:贺舒可)已获得中国国家药监局批准上市,联合核苷(酸)类似物(NAs)用于慢性乙型肝炎病毒感染的功能性治愈,适用于已接受NAs治疗至少6个月、HBV DNA<90 IU/mL、乙型肝炎表面抗原 (HBsAg)≤3000 IU/mL、无肝硬化的慢性乙型肝炎病毒感染成人患者。
